name: Great Yarmouth
title: Great Yarmouth Thickness Measurement | Offshore & Cargo Ships
description: Ultrasonic thickness gauging in Great Yarmouth for supply, wind farm service and jack-up vessels and coasters: hull, tanks, decks and piping in port calls.
h1: UTM for Offshore Energy Vessels and Cargo Ships at Great Yarmouth
intro: Great Yarmouth has served the southern North Sea's energy industry for more than half a century, first gas and now offshore wind, and its quays are busy with supply ships, standby vessels, service operation vessels and installation craft. Alongside them, coasters use the outer harbour and the river berths on the Yare. Gauging here usually fits into a crew change, a maintenance stop or a weather standby. Our technicians travel from India to meet the vessel, with the visit timed to her return to port.
keywords: great yarmouth outer harbour ship inspection

highlights.p: Supply ships, standby vessels and service operation vessels come back to Great Yarmouth on a rota for cargo, fuel and crew. A scope covering deck plating, cargo rails, tank tops and piping can be split across several returns, keeping the same reference points each time.

Jack-up installation and maintenance vessels lying in the outer harbour between projects give access to deck plating, preload tanks, leg-well and jacking-house structure. Magnetic particle testing at highly stressed welds goes alongside the thickness readings where the owner asks for it.

The outer harbour offers deeper water and open quays with no bridges to wait for, while the river berths on the Yare are sheltered but tidal, with strong currents. Which berth the vessel takes decides how long the team has and how she is reached.

port.h: Great Yarmouth: river port, outer harbour and energy base
p: Great Yarmouth stands on a narrow strip of land between the North Sea and the River Yare, with Gorleston on the opposite bank near the river mouth. For centuries the harbour was the river itself, with quays lining both banks of the Yare's last stretch before the sea, and the tidal streams running through its narrow entrance have always demanded respect from ship handlers. In 2009 an outer harbour was opened on the seaward side, enclosed by two rock breakwaters and giving deeper water and berths that are free of the river's currents and the opening road bridges that cross it. Peel Ports operates both parts of the port. Offshore, the approaches are crowded with sandbanks, which is why this coast has a long history of wrecks and why masters take local advice on the channels in.

The town's maritime character changed in the 1960s, when gas was found beneath the southern North Sea and Great Yarmouth became a supply base for the platforms. Supply ships, standby vessels and survey vessels have worked out of the river ever since, and many of the gas fields they serve are now ageing or moving towards decommissioning. Offshore wind has taken up much of the slack: the wind farms off the Norfolk and Suffolk coast are built and maintained from East Anglian ports, and Great Yarmouth handles installation vessels, crew transfer vessels and the larger service operation vessels that stay offshore for weeks at a time. Cargo trades are smaller but steady, with coasters bringing bulk, general and project cargoes to the river and outer harbour quays.

Offshore work follows the weather window. From spring into early autumn the vessels spend as much time at sea as they can, turning round in port for a few hours at a time, and in winter they spend more days alongside waiting for the sea to go down. That makes the winter months the natural season for longer gauging scopes on offshore vessels, and the summer months the time for short, focused visits. Coasters follow their own schedules and keep the river berths moving all year. Whatever the vessel, the question that decides a gauging job here is the same: how long she will be tied up, and which spaces can be emptied and ventilated in that time without affecting her readiness to sail.

facilities.h: Gauging berths in the river and the outer harbour
p: The outer harbour is where large offshore vessels and jack-ups lie between campaigns, and its quays are open, with room for a vehicle carrying equipment and straightforward access to the vessel's deck. The river berths are tighter. The quays on both banks are long-established and well sheltered from the sea, but the current through the harbour is strong, so a ship's gangway and moorings need tending through each tide while the team works on board. Vessels that need docking go elsewhere: smaller craft often to Lowestoft, a short way down the coast, where there is a dry dock with slipways, and larger offshore vessels and cargo ships to yards in other British ports or on the Continent.

Offshore vessels bring their own access questions. Supply ships carry drilling mud, brine, fuel and water in tanks below deck, so tank entry depends on what the tank last held, how it has been cleaned and gas-freed, and an enclosed-space permit issued under the vessel's own system. Crew transfer vessels are usually aluminium catamarans, which calls for the gauge to be set and checked for the alloy rather than steel. On jack-ups, the preload tanks and the structure around the legs are the areas owners most often ask about, and access is planned with the crew because the legs and their jacking systems are working machinery.
list: Outer harbour quays: hull, deck and preload tank gauging on jack-up installation vessels and service operation vessels between campaigns.
River berths on the Yare: supply ship and standby vessel tank, deck and cargo-rail readings during port turnarounds.
Crew transfer vessel berths: bottom and side plating checks on aluminium catamarans, with the gauge set for the alloy.
Cargo quays in the river and outer harbour: hold and hatch cover gauging on coasters working bulk and project cargoes.
Lowestoft dry dock and slipways, a short way south: where smaller offshore craft go for the repairs that Great Yarmouth readings identify.

context.h: Offshore vetting, port state control and an energy coast in transition
p: Foreign-flagged cargo ships at Great Yarmouth come under the Maritime and Coastguard Agency's port state control, which the UK operates in line with the Paris MoU. Many of the offshore vessels working from the port, though, are examined less often by port state control than by their charterers, through OCIMF's Offshore Vessel Inspection Database and the operators' own vetting against industry guidance for offshore marine operations. Those inspectors look at much of the structure a class surveyor would, and one who finds a wasted deck, a weeping tank or a corroded fire main will want to see thickness evidence before the vessel goes back on hire.

The shift from gas to wind changes the fleet as well as the cargo. Supply ships and standby vessels built for the gas fields are reaching ages at which renewal surveys reveal steel work, and owners are deciding whether to invest, convert a vessel for wind farm service or sell her. Newer service operation vessels often have hybrid power and motion-compensated walk-to-work gangways, but their hulls, ballast tanks and sea chests corrode like any other ship's, and a vessel that stays offshore for weeks gives few chances to look at them. Gauging during a port call lets the technical manager follow that structure between dockings.

jobs.h: Typical thickness gauging jobs at Great Yarmouth
jobs.p: Most Great Yarmouth jobs come from offshore vessel operators and their technical managers, with a smaller share from coaster owners. Offshore work is planned around the vessel's rota: the team boards when she comes in, works for the hours or days she is alongside, and continues on her next return if the scope is larger. Cargo jobs look much like those at any small bulk port, built around discharge, the holds and the hatch covers. In both cases we ask early for the vessel's planned port days, because offshore schedules move with the weather and with the wind farm's maintenance programme.
list: Intermediate survey preparation on a platform supply vessel: deck plating under the cargo area, mud and brine tanks, and fire-main piping.
Preload tank and leg-well structure gauging on a jack-up vessel lying in the outer harbour between installation campaigns.
Bow and fender structure checks on an aluminium crew transfer vessel after a season of pushing on to turbine landings.
Condition gauging of an older standby vessel before the owner decides whether to convert her for wind farm work or sell her.
Hold and hatch cover gauging on a coaster discharging project cargo or aggregates at the river quays.

logistics: The team normally flies into London Heathrow or Stansted and continues to Norfolk by rail or road; Norwich Airport, which also handles offshore helicopter traffic, is the nearest airport but has few international routes. The technicians travel from India on UK visas, so for offshore vessels we ask for a range of likely port days rather than a single date. Access to the outer harbour and the river quays is controlled, and the vessel's agent or the operator's marine coordinator arranges passes against each technician's passport and confirms the berth.

faqs.q: Can you gauge an offshore vessel during a short port turnaround at Great Yarmouth?
faqs.a: Yes, if the scope is matched to the stay. A supply vessel in for cargo and crew may be alongside for less than a day, which suits deck plating, cargo rails, air pipes and accessible piping. Tanks have to be emptied, cleaned and gas-freed first, so they are better kept for a longer stay or a weather standby. We agree the priorities with the master and the technical manager and pick up the rest on the next return.

faqs.q: Do you gauge aluminium crew transfer vessels?
faqs.a: Yes. Ultrasonic thickness gauging works on aluminium, but the instrument must be set to the sound velocity of the alloy and checked on a reference block of the same material, otherwise the readings are wrong. On crew transfer vessels we usually look at the bottom and side plating in the bow area, which takes the load each time the vessel pushes on to a turbine landing, and at the fender structure.

faqs.q: Is there a dry dock at Great Yarmouth?
faqs.a: Not one that takes the vessels most often needing gauging. Smaller craft are often docked at Lowestoft, a short distance south, and larger offshore vessels and cargo ships at yards elsewhere in Britain or on the Continent. Gauging at Great Yarmouth is therefore mostly afloat work, either as a pre-docking estimate for that yard or as a condition check between dockings.

faqs.q: Which harbour suits a longer gauging job, the river or the outer harbour?
faqs.a: Where there is a choice, the outer harbour. It has deeper water, no opening bridges and berths that are not affected by the river's tidal currents, so a vessel can lie steady while tanks are opened one after another. The river berths work well for shorter scopes, but moorings and gangway need watching through each tide, and that takes some of the crew's attention away from supporting the inspection.
